In this section “respondent”, in relation to an application for a consumer protection order, means— where the application is for an enforcement order or an interim enforcement order, the person against whom the order is sought; where the application is for an online interface order or an interim online interface order, the person against whom the order is sought or another person who is a party to the proceedings.

commentary.text: S. 180 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: This section applies where the CMA has reasonable grounds for suspecting that— a person has engaged, is engaging or is likely to engage in a commercial practice that constitutes a relevant infringement, or a person is an accessory to such a practice. The CMA may conduct an investigation into the matter. Where the CMA conducts an investigation, it may publish a notice which (among other things) may— state its decision to conduct the investigation, summarise the matter under investigation (including the industry sectors affected), identify, so far as possible, the persons under investigation (including whether they are suspected of falling within subsection (1)(a) or (b)), and indicate the timetable for the conduct of the investigation. If after giving a notice under subsection (3) the CMA decides to close an investigation, the CMA must publish a notice confirming that the investigation is to be closed.

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024

commentary.text: S. 181 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: This section applies where— the CMA has started an investigation under section 180 that is continuing, and the condition in subsection (2) is met in respect of any person (“the respondent”) who is subject to the investigation. The condition in this subsection is met in respect of the respondent if the CMA has reasonable grounds to believe that— the respondent has engaged, is engaging or is likely to engage in a commercial practice constituting a relevant infringement (“the infringing practice”), or the respondent is an accessory to such a practice. The CMA may give to the respondent a notice under this section (a “provisional infringement notice”). A provisional infringement notice must— set out the grounds on which it is given, including the respondent’s acts or omissions giving rise to the CMA’s belief that the condition in subsection (2) is met; set out proposed directions for the purposes of securing that the respondent complies with subsection (5); invite the respondent to make representations to the CMA about the giving of the notice; specify the means by which, and the time by which, such representations must be made. The respondent complies with this subsection by— in the case of a respondent within subsection (2)(a), not continuing or repeating the infringing practice (where it is believed that the respondent has engaged or is engaging in that practice); in the case of a respondent within subsection (2)(b), not consenting to or conniving in the infringing practice; in either case, not engaging in the infringing practice in the course of the respondent’s business or another business; in either case, not consenting to or conniving in the carrying out of the infringing practice by a body corporate with which the respondent has a special relationship (see section 220). If the proposed directions mentioned in subsection (4)(b) include the taking by the respondent of enhanced consumer measures, the notice must state that fact and include details of the proposed measures to be taken (but section 183 applies in respect of any such proposed measures specified in a provisional infringement notice as that section applies to such measures specified in a final infringement notice). The means specified under subsection (4)(d) for making representations must include arrangements for them to be made orally if the respondent chooses to make representations in that way. If the CMA is considering the imposition of a monetary penalty on the respondent (see section 182(4)(b)), the provisional infringement notice must also state— that the CMA is considering imposing a monetary penalty; the proposed amount of the penalty; any further factors (in addition to those provided under subsection (4)(a)) which the CMA considers may justify the imposition of the proposed penalty and its amount.

text: This section applies where— the CMA has given to the respondent a provisional infringement notice under section 181, the time for the respondent to make representations to the CMA in accordance with that notice has expired, and after considering such representations (if any), the CMA is satisfied that— the respondent has engaged, is engaging or is likely to engage in a commercial practice constituting a relevant infringement, or the respondent is an accessory to such a practice. The CMA may give to the respondent a notice under this section (a “final infringement notice”). In deciding whether to give a final infringement notice the CMA must, in particular, have regard to whether the respondent has previously given an undertaking under this Chapter or Chapter 3 in respect of the acts or omissions in relation to which the final infringement notice would be given. A final infringement notice may impose on the respondent a requirement to do either or both of the following— a requirement to comply with such directions as the CMA considers appropriate for or in connection with the purpose of securing that the respondent complies with section 181(5) (which may include directions to take enhanced consumer measures in accordance with section 183); subject to subsection (5), a requirement to pay a monetary penalty. In the case of a respondent within subsection (1)(c)(i), a requirement to pay a monetary penalty may be imposed only if the CMA is satisfied that the respondent has engaged, or is engaging, in a commercial practice constituting a relevant infringement (and not in respect of a practice that the CMA is satisfied that the person is likely to engage in). The amount of a monetary penalty imposed under subsection (4)(b) must be a fixed amount not exceeding £300,000 or, if higher, 10% of the total value of the turnover (if any) of the respondent. A final infringement notice must— set out the grounds on which it is given, including the respondent’s acts or omissions on account of which the notice is given; state any further factors (in addition to those provided under paragraph (a)) which the CMA considers justify the giving of the notice; if a penalty is imposed by the notice under subsection (4)(b), contain the monetary penalty information (see section 203); state that the respondent has a right to appeal against the notice and the main details of that right (so far as not stated in accordance with paragraph (c)). A final infringement notice may require the respondent to publish— the notice; a corrective statement. Publication under subsection (8) must be made in such form and manner, and to such extent, as the CMA considers appropriate for the purpose of eliminating any continuing effects of the relevant infringement.

heading_breadcrumb: Final infringement notice: directions to take enhanced consumer measures

commentary.text: S. 183 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: Directions contained in a final infringement notice may include directions requiring the respondent to take such enhanced consumer measures as the CMA considers just and reasonable. For this purpose, in deciding whether to require the taking of enhanced consumer measures the CMA must in particular consider whether any proposed enhanced consumer measures are proportionate having regard to— the likely benefit of the measures to consumers, the costs likely to be incurred by the respondent, and the likely cost to consumers of obtaining the benefit of the measures. The costs referred to in subsection (2)(b) are— the cost of the measures, and the reasonable administrative costs associated with taking the measures. Where the respondent is required by a final infringement notice to take enhanced consumer measures, the notice may include requirements for the respondent to provide information or documents to the CMA in order that the CMA may determine if the respondent is taking those measures. Subsection (6) applies if— a final infringement notice requires the taking of enhanced consumer measures offering compensation, and a settlement agreement is entered into in connection with the payment of compensation. A waiver of a person’s rights in the settlement agreement is not valid if it is a waiver of the right to bring civil proceedings in respect of conduct other than conduct which has given rise to the final infringement notice.

commentary.text: S. 184 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: This section applies where the CMA is satisfied that a person has engaged, is engaging or is likely to engage in a commercial practice that constitutes a relevant infringement. The CMA may give a notice under this section (an “online interface notice”) to— the person that the CMA is satisfied has engaged, is engaging or is likely to engage in the commercial practice constituting the relevant infringement, or any other person (subject to subsection (3)). A notice under subsection (2)(b) may be given to a person who is outside the United Kingdom only if the person— is a United Kingdom national, is an individual who is habitually resident in the United Kingdom, is a firm established in the United Kingdom, or carries on business in the United Kingdom or by any means directs activities in the course of carrying on a business to consumers in the United Kingdom. An online interface notice may contain whatever directions the CMA considers appropriate for the purpose of requiring the person to whom it is given to do, or to co-operate with another person so that person can do, one or more of the following— remove content from, or modify content on, an online interface; disable or restrict access to an online interface; display a warning to consumers accessing an online interface; delete a fully qualified domain name and take any steps necessary to facilitate the registration of that domain name by the CMA. An online interface notice may be given to a person only if the CMA is satisfied that— there are no other available means under section 162 or under another provision of this Chapter of bringing about the cessation or prohibition of the infringement which, by themselves, would be wholly effective, and it is necessary for the directions contained in the notice to be given to avoid the risk of serious harm to the collective interests of consumers. An online interface notice must— set out the grounds on which it is given; state that the respondent has the right to appeal against the notice and the main details of that right. Where an online interface notice is given, the CMA may publish— the notice, and where known, the identity of the person who has engaged, is engaging or is likely to engage in a commercial practice which constitutes the relevant infringement. Publication under subsection (7) must be made in such form and manner as the CMA considers appropriate for the purpose of eliminating any continuing effects of the relevant infringement. For the purposes of subsection (3)(c), a firm is “established in the United Kingdom” if— it is incorporated or formed under the law of a part of the United Kingdom, or it is administered under arrangements governed by the law of a part of the United Kingdom. In subsection (4) “online interface” means any software, including a website, part of a website, an application or other digital content which— is operated by a person (“P”) acting for purposes relating to P’s business or by a person acting in the name of, or on behalf of, P, and is operated for or in connection with the purposes of giving access to, or promoting, the goods, services or digital content that P or another person supplies.

commentary.text: S. 185 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: This section applies where the CMA— has started an investigation under section 180 which is continuing, and has not given a final infringement notice or an online interface notice in relation to the matter under investigation. The CMA may accept an undertaking under this section in connection with that matter from any person whom the CMA believes— has engaged, is engaging or is likely to engage in a commercial practice that constitutes a relevant infringement (“the infringing practice”), or is an accessory to such a practice. Subsections (1) to (6) of section 164 (inclusion of enhanced consumer measures in undertakings) apply to an undertaking under this section as they apply to an undertaking under section 163(2). An undertaking under this section is an undertaking to do one or more of the following— in the case of an undertaking from a person within subsection (2)(a), not to continue or repeat the infringing practice (where the CMA believes the person has engaged or is engaging in the practice); in the case of an undertaking from a person within subsection (2)(b), not to consent to or connive in the infringing practice; in either case, not to engage in the infringing practice in the course of the person’s business or another business; in either case, not to consent to, or connive in, the carrying out of the infringing practice by a body corporate with which the person has a special relationship (see section 220). Where the CMA has accepted from a person an undertaking under this section— the CMA may accept from the person any such variation of the undertaking that the CMA considers appropriate for meeting the purposes for which the undertaking was given; the CMA may release the person from the undertaking (whether on its own initiative or at the person’s request) if the CMA considers that the undertaking is no longer necessary to further those purposes. The powers of the CMA under this section do not limit other powers of the CMA to accept, vary or release undertakings under Chapter 3.

text: This section applies where the CMA accepts an undertaking from a person under section 185 in connection with a matter that it was investigating under section 180. Subsection (2) does not prevent the CMA from giving a final infringement notice or an online interface notice to the person— if and to the extent that the notice relates to anything not addressed by the acceptance of the undertaking mentioned in subsection (1); if the CMA considers that there has been a material change of circumstances since the undertaking was accepted; if the CMA has reasonable grounds for suspecting that a person from whom the undertaking was accepted has failed to adhere to one or more of the terms of the undertaking; if the CMA has reasonable grounds for suspecting that information which led it to accept the undertaking was incomplete, false or misleading in a material way. text: This section applies where the CMA proposes to— accept a material variation of an undertaking under section 185, or release a person from any such undertaking, and the proposed variation or release has not been requested by the person who gave the undertaking. commentary.text: S. 188 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: This section applies where— the CMA has accepted an undertaking from a person (“the respondent”) under section 185, and the CMA has reasonable grounds to believe that the respondent has failed to comply with one or more of the terms of the undertaking. The CMA may give to the respondent a notice under this section (a “provisional breach of undertakings enforcement notice”). A provisional breach of undertakings enforcement notice must— set out the grounds on which it is given, including the respondent’s alleged acts or omissions giving rise to the belief mentioned in subsection (1)(b); set out proposed directions for the purpose of securing that the respondent complies with subsection (5); invite the respondent to make representations to the CMA about the giving of the notice; specify the means by which, and the time by which, such representations must be made. The means specified under subsection (3)(d) for making representations must include arrangements for them to be made orally if the respondent chooses to make representations in that way. The respondent complies with this subsection by— in the case of a respondent within section 185(2)(a), not continuing or repeating the infringing practice (where it is believed that the respondent has engaged or is engaging in that practice); in the case of a respondent within section 185(2)(b), not consenting to or conniving in the infringing practice; in either case, not engaging in the infringing practice in the course of the respondent’s business or another business; in either case, not consenting to or conniving in the carrying out of the infringing practice by a body corporate with which the respondent has a special relationship (see section 220). If the CMA is considering the imposition of a monetary penalty on the respondent (see section 189(3)(b)), the provisional breach of undertakings enforcement notice must also state— that the CMA is considering imposing a monetary penalty; the proposed amount of the penalty (including whether the penalty would be a fixed amount, an amount calculated by reference to a daily rate or both a fixed amount and an amount calculated by reference to a daily rate); any further factors (in addition to those provided under subsection (3)(a)) which the CMA considers justify the imposition of the proposed penalty and its amount or amounts.

commentary.text: S. 189 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: This section applies where— the CMA has given to the respondent a provisional breach of undertakings enforcement notice under section 188, the time for the respondent to make representations to the CMA in accordance with that notice has expired, and after considering such representations (if any), the CMA is satisfied that the respondent has failed to comply with one or more of the terms of the undertaking. The CMA may give to the respondent a notice under this section (a “final breach of undertakings enforcement notice”). A final breach of undertakings enforcement notice may, subject to subsection (4), impose on the respondent a requirement to do either or both of the following— to comply with such directions as the CMA considers appropriate for the purpose of securing that the respondent complies with section 188(5); to pay a monetary penalty in respect of the failure mentioned in subsection (1)(c). A requirement under subsection (3)(b) to pay a monetary penalty may be imposed only if the CMA is satisfied that the failure in question is without reasonable excuse. A final breach of undertakings enforcement notice must— set out the grounds on which it is given, including the respondent’s acts or omissions giving rise to the failure mentioned in subsection (1)(c); state any further factors (in addition to those provided under paragraph (a)) which the CMA considers justify the giving of the notice; if directions are given under subsection (3)(a), specify the actions to be taken by the respondent in accordance with the directions; if a penalty is imposed under subsection (3)(b), specify the monetary penalty information (see section 203); state that the respondent has a right to appeal against the notice and the main details of that right (so far as not stated in accordance with paragraph (d)). The CMA may publish a final breach of undertakings enforcement notice in such manner, and to such extent, as the CMA considers appropriate.

commentary.text: S. 190 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: This section applies in relation to a requirement imposed on the respondent to pay a monetary penalty under a final breach of undertakings enforcement notice. The amount of the penalty must be— a fixed amount, an amount calculated by reference to a daily rate, or a combination of a fixed amount and an amount calculated by reference to a daily rate. The penalty must not exceed— in the case of a fixed amount, £150,000 or, if higher, 5% of the total value of the turnover (if any) of the respondent; in the case of an amount calculated by reference to a daily rate, for each day £15,000 or, if higher, 5% of the total value of the daily turnover (if any) of the respondent; in the case of a fixed amount and an amount calculated by reference to a daily rate, such fixed amount and such amount per day. In imposing a penalty by reference to a daily rate— no account is to be taken of any days before the date on which the provisional breach of undertakings enforcement notice was given to the respondent, and unless the CMA determines an earlier date, the amount payable ceases to accumulate on the day on which the requirements of the final breach of undertakings enforcement notice are complied with.

Ss. 191-196 applied (24.5.2024 for specified purposes, 6.4.2025 in so far as not already in force) by 2015 c. 15, Sch. 5 para. 16C(11) (as inserted by Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (c. 13), s. 339(2)(c), Sch. 17 para. 2(3) (with Sch. 19); S.I. 2025/272, reg. 2(1)(8))

text: This section applies where— an enforcement direction has been given to a person (“the respondent”), and the CMA has reasonable grounds to believe that the respondent has without reasonable excuse failed to comply with the direction (fully or to any respect). The CMA may give to the respondent a notice under this section (a “provisional breach of directions enforcement notice”). A provisional breach of directions enforcement notice must— set out the grounds on which it is given, including the respondent’s acts or omissions giving rise to the belief mentioned in subsection (1)(b); set out proposed directions for the purpose of securing that the respondent complies with the direction; invite the respondent to make representations to the CMA about the giving of the notice; specify the means by which, and the time by which, such representations must be made. The means specified under subsection (3)(d) for making representations must include arrangements for them to be made orally if the respondent chooses to make representations in that way. A provisional breach of directions enforcement notice must also state— that the CMA is considering imposing a monetary penalty; the proposed amount of the penalty (including whether the penalty would be a fixed amount, an amount calculated by reference to a daily rate or both a fixed amount and an amount calculated by reference to a daily rate); any further factors (in addition to those provided under subsection (3)(a)) which the CMA considers justify the imposition of the proposed penalty and its amount or amounts. In this Chapter “enforcement direction” means a direction given in— a final infringement notice, an online interface notice, or a final breach of undertakings enforcement notice.

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.
heading_breadcrumb: Final breach of directions enforcement notice

commentary.text: S. 192 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

Ss. 191-196 applied (24.5.2024 for specified purposes, 6.4.2025 in so far as not already in force) by 2015 c. 15, Sch. 5 para. 16C(11) (as inserted by Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (c. 13), s. 339(2)(c), Sch. 17 para. 2(3) (with Sch. 19); S.I. 2025/272, reg. 2(1)(8))

text: This section applies where— the CMA has given to the respondent a provisional breach of directions enforcement notice under section 191 in respect of a suspected failure to comply with an enforcement direction, the time for the respondent to make representations to the CMA in accordance with that notice has expired, and after considering such representations (if any), the CMA is satisfied that the respondent has, without reasonable excuse, failed to comply with the direction. The CMA may give to the respondent a notice under this section (a “final breach of directions enforcement notice”). A final breach of directions enforcement notice is a notice that imposes on the respondent a requirement to pay a monetary penalty. A final breach of directions enforcement notice must— set out the grounds on which it is given, including the respondent’s acts or omissions giving rise to the failure mentioned in subsection (1)(c); state any further factors (in addition to those provided under paragraph (a)) which the CMA considers justify the giving of the notice; specify the monetary penalty information (see section 203). A final breach of directions enforcement notice may— vary or revoke the enforcement direction mentioned in subsection (1); specify such other directions as the CMA considers appropriate for the purpose of securing that the respondent complies with the requirements in respect of which the enforcement direction was given. Where a final breach of directions enforcement notice includes provision under subsection (5) that varies an enforcement direction or specifies other directions, the notice must (in addition to the requirements under subsection (4)) also state that the respondent has a right to appeal against the notice and the main details of that right. The CMA may publish a final breach of directions enforcement notice in such manner, and to such extent, as the CMA considers appropriate.

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.

commentary.text: S. 193 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

Ss. 191-196 applied (24.5.2024 for specified purposes, 6.4.2025 in so far as not already in force) by 2015 c. 15, Sch. 5 para. 16C(11) (as inserted by Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (c. 13), s. 339(2)(c), Sch. 17 para. 2(3) (with Sch. 19); S.I. 2025/272, reg. 2(1)(8))

text: This section applies in relation to a requirement imposed on the respondent to pay a monetary penalty under a final breach of directions enforcement notice. The amount of the penalty must be— a fixed amount, an amount calculated by reference to a daily rate, or a combination of a fixed amount and an amount calculated by reference to a daily rate. The penalty imposed on a person must not exceed— in the case of a fixed amount, £150,000 or, if higher, 5% of the total value of the turnover (if any) of the respondent; in the case of an amount calculated by reference to a daily rate, for each day £15,000 or, if higher, 5% of the total value of the daily turnover (if any) of the respondent; in the case of a fixed amount and an amount calculated by reference to a daily rate, such fixed amount and such amount per day. In imposing a penalty by reference to a daily rate— no account is to be taken of any days before the date on which the provisional breach of directions enforcement notice was given to the respondent, and unless the CMA determines an earlier date, the amount payable ceases to accumulate on the day on which the relevant directions are fully complied with. In subsection (4)(b) the “relevant directions” are— the enforcement direction mentioned in section 192(1)(a) (if not revoked under section 192(5)(a)); any further directions specified under section 192(5)(b).

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.
heading_breadcrumb: Powers of court to enforce directions

commentary.text: S. 194 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

Ss. 191-196 applied (24.5.2024 for specified purposes, 6.4.2025 in so far as not already in force) by 2015 c. 15, Sch. 5 para. 16C(11) (as inserted by Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (c. 13), s. 339(2)(c), Sch. 17 para. 2(3) (with Sch. 19); S.I. 2025/272, reg. 2(1)(8))

text: This section applies where the CMA considers that a person (“the respondent”) has failed to comply with— an enforcement direction, or a direction given in a final breach of directions enforcement notice under section 192(5)(b). The CMA may make an application to the appropriate court under this section. If on an application under subsection (2) the court finds that the respondent has failed to comply with the direction concerned, the court may make an order imposing such requirements on the respondent as the court considers appropriate for the purpose of remedying the failure. An order under this section may provide for all of the costs or expenses of, and incidental to, the application for the order to be met by the respondent or any officer of a person that is responsible for the respondent’s failure to comply with the direction. Nothing in this section limits the powers of the court to make orders under Chapter 3 or otherwise (and an application under this section may be combined with an application under that Chapter for a consumer protection order). The following provisions of Chapter 3 apply to an order under this section as if the order were a consumer protection order— section 173 (appropriate court); section 174 (effect of orders in other parts of the United Kingdom); section 178 (substantiation of claims).

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.

commentary.text: S. 195 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

Ss. 191-196 applied (24.5.2024 for specified purposes, 6.4.2025 in so far as not already in force) by 2015 c. 15, Sch. 5 para. 16C(11) (as inserted by Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (c. 13), s. 339(2)(c), Sch. 17 para. 2(3) (with Sch. 19); S.I. 2025/272, reg. 2(1)(8))

text: This section applies where— the CMA gives a provisional notice under this Chapter to a person (“the respondent”) in respect of a relevant infringement involving a contravention of Chapter 1 of Part 4 (protection from unfair trading), and the respondent makes representations to the CMA in response to that notice. The CMA may, for the purpose of considering the representations, require the respondent to provide evidence as to the accuracy of any factual claim made as part of a commercial practice of the respondent. The CMA may determine that a factual claim of the respondent is inaccurate if— the respondent fails to provide evidence of the accuracy of the claim in response to a requirement imposed under subsection (2), or the CMA considers that any such evidence that is provided is inadequate. In this section “provisional notice” means— a provisional infringement notice, a provisional breach of undertakings enforcement notice, or a provisional breach of directions enforcement notice.

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.

commentary.text: S. 196 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

Ss. 191-196 applied (24.5.2024 for specified purposes, 6.4.2025 in so far as not already in force) by 2015 c. 15, Sch. 5 para. 16C(11) (as inserted by Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (c. 13), s. 339(2)(c), Sch. 17 para. 2(3) (with Sch. 19); S.I. 2025/272, reg. 2(1)(8))

text: This section applies where the CMA proposes to— make a material variation of an enforcement direction given to a person (“the respondent”), or revoke any such direction. Before taking the proposed action mentioned in subsection (1) the CMA must— give notice to the respondent under subsection (3), and consider any representations made in accordance with the notice. A notice under this subsection must state— the fact that CMA is proposing to act as mentioned in subsection (1), the reasons for doing so, and the means by which, and the time by which, representations may be made in relation to the proposed variation or revocation. If after considering any representations made in accordance with a notice under subsection (3) the CMA decides to take the action mentioned in subsection (1), the CMA must give notice to the respondent of that decision. The reference in subsection (1)(a) to a material variation is a reference to any variation that the CMA considers to be material in any respect. In this section “enforcement direction” includes a direction given in a notice under section 192(5)(b).

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.

commentary.text: S. 197 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: This section applies if— the CMA has reasonable grounds to believe that a person (“the respondent”) has, without reasonable excuse, provided information to the CMA that is materially false or misleading, and the information was provided in connection with the carrying out by the CMA of a direct enforcement function. The CMA may give to the respondent a notice under this section (a “provisional false information enforcement notice”). A provisional false information enforcement notice must— set out the grounds on which it is given; state that the CMA is considering imposing a monetary penalty; state the proposed amount of the penalty; state any further factors (in addition to those provided under paragraph (a)) which the CMA considers justify the imposition of the proposed penalty and its amount; invite the respondent to make representations to the CMA about the giving of the notice; specify the means by which, and the time by which, such representations must be made. The means specified under subsection (3)(f) for making representations must include arrangements for them to be made orally if the respondent chooses to make representations in that way. In this Part “direct enforcement function” means— a function of the CMA under this Chapter, or a function of the CMA under paragraph 16B or 16C of Schedule 5 to CRA 2015.

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.

commentary.text: S. 198 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: This section applies where— the CMA has given to the respondent a provisional false information enforcement notice under section 197 in connection with the provision of information, the time for the respondent to make representations to the CMA in accordance with the notice has expired, and after considering such representations (if any), the CMA is satisfied that— the information mentioned in paragraph (a) is materially false or misleading, and the respondent provided the false or misleading information without reasonable excuse. The CMA may give to the respondent a notice under this section (“a final false information enforcement notice”). A final false information enforcement notice is a notice that imposes on the respondent a requirement to pay a monetary penalty. The amount of the penalty must be a fixed amount not exceeding £30,000 or, if higher, 1% of the total value of the turnover (if any) of the respondent. A final false information enforcement notice must— set out the grounds on which it is given; state any further factors (in addition to those provided under paragraph (a)) which the CMA considers justify the giving of the notice; specify the monetary penalty information (see section 203). The CMA may publish a final false information enforcement notice in such manner, and to such extent, as the CMA considers appropriate.

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.
heading_breadcrumb: Statement of policy in relation to monetary penalties

commentary.text: S. 199 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: The CMA must prepare and publish a statement of policy in relation to the exercise of powers to impose a monetary penalty under this Chapter. The statement must include a statement about the considerations relevant to the determination of— whether to impose a penalty under this Chapter, and the nature and amount of any such penalty. The CMA may revise its statement of policy and, where it does so, must publish the revised statement. In preparing or revising its statement of policy the CMA must consult— the Secretary of State, and such other persons as the CMA considers appropriate. A statement of policy, or revised statement, may not be published under this section without the approval of the Secretary of State. Subsection (7) applies where the CMA proposes to impose under this Chapter a monetary penalty on a person. The CMA must have regard to the statement of policy most recently published under this section at the time of the act or omission giving rise to the penalty in deciding— whether to impose the penalty, and if so, the nature and amount of the penalty.

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.

commentary.text: S. 200 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: This section applies where— the CMA gives to a body corporate (“the respondent”) a final notice, and the interconnection condition applies in relation to the respondent. The interconnection condition applies in relation to the respondent if— at the time the final notice is given, the respondent is a member of a group of interconnected bodies corporate, at any time when requirements imposed by the final notice remain in force, the respondent becomes a member of a group of interconnected bodies corporate, or at any time when requirements imposed by the final notice remain in force, a group of interconnected bodies corporate of which the respondent is a member is increased by the addition of one or more further members. The notice may include provision for the requirements (or any particular requirements) imposed by the final notice on the respondent also to be binding upon all other members of the group (in addition to the respondent), as if each of them were the respondent. Provision may be included in a notice under subsection (3) only if the CMA considers it just, reasonable and proportionate to include that provision. A group of interconnected bodies corporate is a group consisting of two or more bodies corporate all of whom are interconnected with each other. Any two bodies corporate are interconnected— if one of them is a subsidiary of the other, or if both of them are subsidiaries of the same body corporate. Where a final notice includes provision under subsection (3), the notice must also be given to any other member of the respondent’s group in relation to which the requirements imposed by the notice are to be binding. In this section “final notice” means— a final infringement notice, an online interface notice, or a final breach of directions enforcement notice.

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.

commentary.text: S. 201 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: The CMA must keep a record of— undertakings it has accepted and enforcement directions it has given, and reviews it has carried out in relation to the effectiveness of such undertakings and directions. If requested to do so by the Secretary of State, the CMA must prepare a report on— the effectiveness of undertakings and enforcement directions, and the number and outcome of appeals brought under section 202. The CMA must— provide to the Secretary of State a report prepared under this section, and publish the report in such manner as the CMA considers appropriate. In this section— “undertakings” means undertakings given under section 185; “enforcement directions” includes directions given in a notice under section 192(5)(b).

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.

commentary.text: S. 202 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: A person to whom a relevant notice is given may appeal to the appropriate appeal court against— a decision to impose a monetary penalty by virtue of the notice, the nature or amount of any such penalty, or the giving of directions by virtue of the notice. The grounds for an appeal under subsection (1)(a) or (b) are that— the decision to impose a monetary penalty was based on an error of fact, the decision was wrong in law, the amount of the penalty is unreasonable, or the decision was unreasonable or wrong for any other reason. The grounds for an appeal under subsection (1)(c) are that— the decision to give the directions was based on an error of fact, the decision was wrong in law, the nature of the directions is unreasonable, or the decision was unreasonable or wrong for any other reason. On an appeal under this section the appropriate appeal court may quash, confirm or vary the relevant notice. Except in the case of an appeal relating to a final false information enforcement notice, in addition to the powers conferred by subsection (4) the appropriate appeal court may also remit any matter that is the subject of the appeal to the CMA. An appeal under this section must be brought before the end of the applicable period beginning with the day on which the relevant notice was given to the person seeking to bring the appeal. The appropriate appeal court may extend the applicable period for bringing an appeal. Where an appeal is brought in respect of— a requirement to pay a monetary penalty, or a requirement to pay compensation under directions imposing enhanced consumer measures, the penalty or compensation is not required to be paid until after the appeal is determined, withdrawn or otherwise dealt with. In this section— “applicable period” means— in relation to a final false information enforcement notice, the period of 28 days; in relation to any other relevant notice, the period of 60 days; “appropriate appeal court” means— in relation to England and Wales or Northern Ireland, the High Court; in relation to Scotland, the Outer House of the Court of Session; “relevant notice” means— a final infringement notice, an online interface notice, a final breach of undertakings enforcement notice, a final breach of directions enforcement notice, or a final false information enforcement notice.

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.
heading_breadcrumb: Information to accompany orders or notices imposing monetary penalties

commentary.text: S. 203 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: An order or notice under Chapter 3 or 4 under which a person (“the respondent”) is required to pay a monetary penalty must state the following information (referred to in those Chapters as the “monetary penalty information”)— the amount of the penalty (including whether it is a fixed amount, an amount calculated by reference to a daily rate or both a fixed amount and an amount calculated by reference to a daily rate); the grounds on which the penalty is imposed together with any other factors that the court (in the case of an order) or the CMA (in the case of a notice) considers justify the giving of the penalty or its amount; in the case of an amount calculated by reference to a daily rate, the day on which the amount first starts to accumulate and the day or days on which it might cease to accumulate; how the penalty is to be paid; the date or dates, no earlier than the end of the applicable period beginning with the date on which the order was served on or the notice was given to the respondent, by which the penalty or (as the case may be) different portions of it are required to be paid; that the penalty or (as the case may be) different portions of it may be paid earlier than the date or dates by which it or they are required to be paid; that the respondent has the right to apply under subsection (3) (in the case of an order) or subsection (4) (in the case of a notice); the rights available to the respondent to appeal in respect of the imposition of the penalty; the main details of the rights mentioned in paragraphs (g) and (h). In subsection (1)(e) “the applicable period” means— in the case of an order or a final false information enforcement notice, the period of 28 days; in any other case, the period of 60 days. The respondent may, within 14 days of the date on which an order imposing a monetary penalty is served on the respondent, apply to the court for the court to specify a different date or dates by which the penalty, or different portions of it, are to be paid. The respondent may, within 14 days of the date on which a notice imposing a monetary penalty is given to the respondent, apply to the CMA to specify a different date or dates by which the penalty, or different portions of it, are required to be paid. References in subsections (1) and (2) to an order include references to a notice accompanying such an order given under section 158(4). In the application of this section to Scotland, the references in subsections (1)(e) and (3) to an order being served include service of an extract order in execution of or diligence on the order.

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.

commentary.text: S. 204 in force at Royal Assent for specified purposes, see s. 339(2)(c)
S. 204 in force at 6.4.2025 in so far as not already in force by S.I. 2025/272, reg. 2(1)(2)

text: In this Part references to “turnover” of a person include— turnover both in and outside the United Kingdom; where the person controls another person, the turnover of that other person; where the person is controlled by another person, the turnover of that person. The Secretary of State may by regulations— make provision for determining when a person is to be treated as controlled by another person for the purposes of subsection (1)(b) and (c); make provision for determining the turnover of a person for the purposes of this Part. Regulations under this section may, in particular, make provision as to— the amounts which are, or which are not, to be treated as comprising a person’s turnover or daily turnover; the date or dates by reference to which a person’s turnover or daily turnover is to be determined. Regulations under this section may include provision enabling the court or the CMA to determine matters of a description specified in the regulations (including any of the matters mentioned in paragraphs (a) and (b) of subsection (3)). Regulations under this section are subject to the negative procedure.

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.

commentary.text: S. 205 in force at Royal Assent for specified purposes, see s. 339(2)(c)
S. 205 in force at 6.4.2025 in so far as not already in force by S.I. 2025/272, reg. 2(1)(2)

text: The Secretary of State may by regulations amend any of the following provisions for the purpose of substituting a different monetary amount for an amount of fixed or daily penalty for the time being specified— section 158(5); section 168(3)(a) and (b); section 182(6); section 190(3)(a) and (b); section 193(3)(a) and (b); section 198(4). Before making regulations under this section the Secretary of State must consult such persons as the Secretary of State considers appropriate. Regulations under this section are subject to the affirmative procedure.

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.

commentary.text: S. 206 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: This section applies where a monetary penalty imposed under Chapter 4, or any part of such a penalty, has not been paid by the date on which it is required to be paid and— an appeal to a court against the imposition of the penalty has not been brought before the end of the period within which it is required to be brought, or any such appeal that was brought has been determined, withdrawn or otherwise disposed of. The CMA may recover from the person on whom the penalty was imposed any of the penalty and any interest which has not been paid. Any such penalty and interest may be recovered summarily (or, in Scotland, recovered) as a civil debt by the CMA. Subsection (5) applies where— a penalty is payable by a person by virtue of a final infringement notice, the notice also includes directions imposing a requirement on the person to take enhanced consumer measures, and the enhanced consumer measures that the person is required to take are or include redress measures (see section 221(2)). In deciding whether to recover the penalty from the person under subsection (2), the CMA must have regard to— whether any compensation required to be paid to consumers under the redress measures has been, or is likely to be, paid, and where any such payments have not yet been paid (in full or in part), the effect that recovery of the penalty from the person may have on the person’s ability to make those compensatory payments.

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.

commentary.text: S. 207 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: If the whole or any portion of a monetary penalty imposed is not paid by the date by which it is required to be paid, the unpaid balance from time to time carries interest at the statutory rate. Where an application has been made under section 203(3) or (4), the penalty is not required to be paid until the application has been determined, withdrawn or otherwise disposed of. Where an application has been made to appeal to a court in respect of a monetary penalty, the penalty is not required to be paid until the application has been determined, withdrawn or otherwise disposed of. If a portion of a monetary penalty imposed by an order of the court has not been paid by the date required for it, the court may, where it considers it appropriate to do so, by order require so much of the penalty as has not already been paid (and is capable of being paid immediately) to be paid immediately. If a portion of a monetary penalty imposed by virtue of a notice given by the CMA has not been paid by the date required for it, the CMA may, where it considers it appropriate to do so, by notice require so much of the penalty as has not already been paid (and is capable of being paid immediately) to be paid immediately. Where on an appeal under section 202 the court substitutes a penalty of a different nature or of a lesser amount, the court may require the payment of interest at the statutory rate on the substituted penalty from whatever date it considers appropriate (which may include a date before the determination of the appeal). In the case of a monetary penalty imposed on a firm that is not a body corporate, the penalty is to be paid out of the assets or funds of the firm. Sums received from a person towards payment of a monetary penalty must be paid— in the case of a penalty imposed by an order of the Court of Session or the Sheriff, into the Scottish Consolidated Fund; in the case of a penalty imposed by an order of a court in Northern Ireland, into the Consolidated Fund of Northern Ireland; in any other case, into the Consolidated Fund of the United Kingdom. In this section— “monetary penalty” means a monetary penalty imposed under Chapter 3 or 4; “the statutory rate” means the rate for the time being specified in section 17 of the Judgments Act 1838.

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.

commentary.text: S. 208 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: Schedule 17 contains amendments to Schedule 5 to CRA 2015 (investigatory powers), including amendments about— the giving of monetary penalties in connection with a failure to comply with an information notice; the giving of information notices to persons outside the United Kingdom; the means by which information notices are to be given; entry to premises where documents are accessible from the premises. In subsection (1) “information notice” means a notice given under paragraph 14 of Schedule 5 to CRA 2015.

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.

commentary.text: S. 209 in force at Royal Assent for specified purposes, see s. 339(2)(c)
S. 209 in force at 6.4.2025 in so far as not already in force by S.I. 2025/272, reg. 2(1)(2)

text: The Secretary of State may by regulations amend— the first column of the Table in Part 1 of Schedule 15 so as to add, remove or vary an entry for an enactment; the second column of that Table so as to add, remove or vary an entry providing for the authorised enforcers in respect of an enactment; the third column of that Table in consequence of amendments made under the power conferred by paragraph (a); the second column of the Table in Part 2 of Schedule 15 so as to add, remove or vary an entry providing for the authorised enforcers in respect of an obligation or rule of law; Schedule 16 so as to add, remove or vary an entry for an enactment. The power under subsection (1)(a) or (e) is exercisable so as to add or vary an entry in respect of an enactment only if, and to the extent that, one or more of the following is provided for under or by virtue of the enactment so added or varied— a duty, prohibition or restriction enforceable by criminal proceedings; a duty owed to a person that is enforceable by civil proceedings; a remedy or sanction enforceable by civil proceedings; an agreement or security relating to a supply of goods, services or digital content to be void or unenforceable to any extent; a right or remedy exercisable by a person supplying goods, services or digital content to be restricted or excluded; the avoidance (to any extent) of liability relating to the supply of goods, services or digital content to be restricted or prevented. It is immaterial for the purposes of subsection (2) whether or not— a duty, prohibition or restriction exists in relation to consumers as such; a remedy or sanction is provided for the benefit of consumers as such; proceedings have been brought in relation to the act or omission concerned; a person has been convicted of an offence in relation to the act or omission concerned. Regulations under this section are subject to the affirmative procedure.

commentary.text: S. 217 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: This section provides for how references to the supply of goods or digital content are to be read for the purposes of this Part. References to a person who supplies goods or digital content are to be read as including references to a person who seeks to supply goods or digital content (and references to a person who receives goods or digital content are to be read in a corresponding way). The supply of goods includes, in relation to buildings and other structures, construction of them by one person for another. References to a person supplying goods under— a hire-purchase agreement, a credit-sale agreement, or a conditional sale agreement, are to be read as including references to a person who conducts any antecedent negotiations relating to the agreement. The following terms have the meanings given by section 189(1) of the Consumer Credit Act 1974— “antecedent negotiations”; “conditional sale agreement”; “credit sale agreement”; “hire-purchase agreement”.

text: This section provides for how references to the supply of services are to be read for the purposes of this Part. The supply of services does not include the provision of services under a contract of service or of apprenticeship. It is immaterial whether the contract mentioned in subsection (3)— is express or implied, or if express, is oral or in writing. The supply of services includes— performing for gain or reward any activity other than the supply of goods or digital content; rendering services to order; the provision of services by making them available to potential users; making arrangements for sharing the use of electronic communications apparatus by means of a relevant agreement, within the meaning of paragraph 18 of Schedule 3A to the Communications Act 2003 (the electronic communications code); agreeing to the full or partial settlement of a consumer’s liabilities or purported liabilities in return for the consumer meeting a demand for payment.

text: This section applies for the purposes of this Part. long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.

commentary.text: S. 220 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: This section applies for the purposes of this Part. A person has a special relationship with a body corporate if the person is— a controller of the body corporate, or a director, manager, secretary or other similar officer of the body corporate or a person purporting to act in such a capacity. A person is a controller of a body corporate if— the directors of the body corporate, or of another body corporate which is its controller, are accustomed to act in accordance with the person’s directions or instructions, or either alone or with one or more associates, the person is entitled to exercise or control the exercise of one third or more of the voting power at any general meeting of the body corporate or of another body corporate which is its controller. A person (“P”) is an associate of an individual if— P is the spouse or civil partner of the individual; P is a relative of the individual; P is a relative of the individual’s spouse or civil partner; P is the spouse or civil partner of a relative of the individual; P is a spouse or civil partner of a relative of the individual’s spouse or civil partner; P lives in the same household as the individual otherwise than merely because P, or the individual, is the other’s employer, tenant, lodger or boarder; P is the relative of a person who is an associate of the individual by virtue of paragraph (f); P has at some time in the past fallen within any of paragraphs (a) to (g); P is in partnership with the individual; the individual is an associate of an individual with whom P is in partnership. A person (“P”) is an associate of a body corporate if— P is a controller of the body corporate, or P is an associate of a person who is a controller of the body corporate. A body corporate is an associate of another body corporate if— the same person is a controller of both; a person (“P”) is a controller of one and persons who are P’s associates are controllers of the other; a person (“P”) is a controller of one and P and persons who are P’s associates are controllers of the other; a group of two or more persons is a controller of each company and the groups consist of the same persons; a group of two or more persons is a controller of each company and the groups may be regarded as consisting of the same persons by treating (in one or more cases) a member of either group as replaced by a person of whom that person is an associate. In this section “relative” means a brother, sister, uncle, aunt, nephew, niece, lineal ancestor or lineal descendant.

commentary.text: S. 221 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: References in this Part to “enhanced consumer measures” are references to— redress measures (see subsection (2)), compliance measures (see subsection (3)), or choice measures (see subsection (4)). Redress measures are— measures offering compensation or other redress to affected consumers; in cases where the commercial practice constituting a relevant infringement relates to a contract, measures enabling affected consumers the option to terminate (but not vary) the contract; in cases where the affected consumers cannot be identified, or cannot be identified without disproportionate cost to the person giving the undertaking in question or against whom the order in question is made, measures intended to be in the collective interests of consumers. Compliance measures are measures intended to prevent, or reduce the risk of the occurrence or repetition of, the infringing conduct (which may include measures imposed for the purpose of improving compliance with consumer law more generally). Choice measures are measures intended to enable consumers to choose more effectively between persons supplying goods, services or digital content. In this section— references to affected consumers are references to consumers who have suffered loss as a result of the infringing conduct or who have otherwise been affected in any other way by the conduct; references to the “infringing conduct” are to the conduct that has given rise to the enforcement order or undertaking concerned.
