commentary.text: S. 255 in force at Royal Assent for specified purposes, see s. 339(2)(c)

text: A contract is an excluded contract for the purposes of this Chapter if, and to the extent that, it is of a description set out in Schedule 22. The Secretary of State may by regulations amend Schedule 22 so as to add, remove or modify a description of a contract. The power under subsection (2) includes power to provide for a contract to be an excluded contract— generally for the purposes of this Chapter, or only for such purposes of this Chapter as are specified. Regulations under subsection (2) are subject to the affirmative procedure. See section 275(4) to (8) for how this Chapter applies in relation to a contract that— was an excluded contract at the time it was entered into, and on subsequently ceasing to be an excluded contract, becomes a subscription contract.

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.

commentary.text: S. 256 in force at Royal Assent for specified purposes, see s. 339(2)(c)

text: Before a trader enters into a subscription contract with a consumer, the trader must— give to the consumer the information set out in Part 1 of Schedule 23 (“key pre-contract information”), and give, or make available, to the consumer the information set out in Part 2 of Schedule 23 (“full pre-contract information”). The duty imposed by subsection (1) must be carried out— as close in time to entering into the contract as is practicable, in accordance with subsections (3) and (4), and in accordance with any other requirements specified in regulations under section 277(1)(a). Key pre-contract information must be given under subsection (1)(a) in accordance with the following requirements— it must all be given together; it must be given separately from the full pre-contract information and any other information; in relation to a contract entered into in person, it must be given in writing and on a durable medium; in relation to a contract entered into online and remotely (but not orally), it must be given in writing and in such a way that the consumer is not required to take any steps to read the information, other than the steps the consumer must take to enter into the contract; in relation to a contract entered into orally and remotely, it must be given orally. Full pre-contract information must be given, or made available, under subsection (1)(b) in accordance with the following requirements— it must all be given, or made available, together; in relation to a contract entered into in person, it must be given in writing and on a durable medium. The duty under subsection (1)(b) to give, or make available, full pre-contract information applies in relation to the information set out in paragraphs 14 to 28 of Schedule 23 only to the extent that the information is applicable to the contract and not already apparent from the context. For the purposes of this section, information is made available to a consumer only if the consumer can reasonably be expected to— know how to access it, and be able to access it; For the purposes of this Chapter— references to a contract being entered into in person are references to it being entered into in the simultaneous physical presence of the trader and the consumer; references to a contract being entered into remotely are references to it being entered into without the simultaneous physical presence of the trader and the consumer. The Secretary of State may by regulations amend Parts 1 and 2 of Schedule 23 so as to add, modify or remove descriptions of information. Regulations under subsection (8) are subject to the affirmative procedure.

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.

commentary.text: S. 257 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: Subsections (2) and (3) apply in relation to a subscription contract entered into online. The trader must ensure that the final step which the consumer is required to take to enter into the contract involves the consumer expressly acknowledging that the contract imposes an obligation on the consumer to make payments to the trader. The trader must ensure that the information mentioned in subsection (4) is given to a consumer— in writing and in such a way that the consumer is not required to take any steps to read the information, other than the steps the consumer must take to enter into the contract, and in accordance with any other requirement specified in regulations under section 277(1)(a). The information referred to in subsection (3) is— whether there are any restrictions on the delivery of the product to be supplied under the contract, and which means of payment are accepted in relation to the product. If the trader does not comply with subsection (2), the consumer is not bound by the subscription contract. Subsection (7) applies in relation to a subscription contract entered into orally and remotely. If a trader contacts the consumer, the trader must, from the outset, disclose— the trader’s identity, where applicable, the identity of the person on whose behalf the trader is making contact, and the commercial purpose of making contact with the consumer. In cases where— the contract has been entered into in person, and the consumer has signed the contract, the trader must give to the consumer a copy of the signed contract immediately after the consumer has signed the contract. In cases where full pre-contract information has not been given under section 256(1)(b) in writing on a durable medium before the contract is entered into, the trader must give the consumer that information in writing on a durable medium as soon as reasonably practicable after the contract has been entered into and— where goods are to be supplied under the contract, before the supply of any goods; where services are to be supplied under the contract, before the supply of any service.

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.

commentary.text: S. 258 in force at Royal Assent for specified purposes, see s. 339(2)(c)

text: Where a trader enters into a subscription contract with a consumer that does not include a concessionary period, the trader must give to the consumer a notice (referred to in this Chapter as a “reminder notice”) in respect of each renewal payment that relates to the end of a relevant six-month period. A “relevant six-month period” for the purposes of subsection (1) is— the period of 6 months beginning with the day after the day on which the contract was entered into, and each subsequent period of 6 months beginning with the day after the day on which the consumer last became liable for a renewal payment in respect of which a reminder notice was required under subsection (1). Where a trader enters into a subscription contract with a consumer that includes a concessionary period, the trader must give to the consumer a reminder notice in respect of— the first renewal payment for which the consumer will become liable under the contract, and each subsequent renewal payment that relates to the end of a relevant six-month period. A “relevant six-month period” for the purposes of subsection (3) is each period of 6 months beginning with the day after the day on which the consumer last became liable for a renewal payment in respect of which a reminder notice was required under subsection (3). A renewal payment “relates” to the end of a relevant six-month period for the purposes of subsections (1) and (3) if— it is the last (or only) renewal payment for which the consumer becomes liable during that period, or in a case where the consumer does not become liable for any renewal payment during that period, it is the first renewal payment for which the consumer becomes liable after the end of that period. For the purposes of this section a subscription contract includes a concessionary period if it is a contract to which section 254(3) applies. In this Chapter, a “renewal payment”, in relation to a subscription contract, means a payment for which the consumer could avoid liability by exercising a right to bring the contract to an end. Section 259 contains further provision about— the contents of reminder notices, the times at which they must be given, and how they must be given. The Secretary of State may by regulations provide for the requirements imposed by this section and section 259— not to apply in relation to specified descriptions of traders or contracts; to apply subject to modifications in relation to specified descriptions of traders or contracts. Regulations under subsection (9) are subject to the affirmative procedure.

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.
heading_breadcrumb: Content and timing etc of reminder notices

commentary.text: S. 259 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: A reminder notice must contain— the information set out in Part 3 of Schedule 23, and any other information required by regulations under section 277(1)(b), and that information must be given to the consumer all together. A reminder notice must be given— in accordance with subsections (3) to (8), in such a way that the information referred to in subsection (1) is more prominent than any other information given to the consumer at the same time, and in accordance with any other requirements specified in regulations under section 277(1)(a). A reminder notice must be given within the period specified by the trader for the purposes of this section in the key pre-contract information given to the consumer in relation to the contract (see paragraph 10 of Schedule 23). A period specified in key pre-contract information for the purposes of this section must be a period in advance of the last cancellation date which is reasonable for the purposes of— informing the consumer that they will soon become liable for the renewal payment to which the notice relates, and enabling the consumer to decide whether to bring the subscription contract to an end before incurring that liability (and to take the necessary steps to do so). The “last cancellation date”, in relation to a reminder notice, means the last day on which the consumer could avoid becoming liable for the renewal payment to which the notice relates by exercising a right to bring the contract to an end. Where subsection (7) applies, in addition to giving a reminder notice in accordance with subsection (3), an additional reminder notice must be given— prior to the notice given in accordance with subsection (3), and at a time which is reasonable for the purpose of providing additional notification to the consumer that they will soon become liable for the renewal payment to which the notice relates. This subsection applies where— the consumer will not become liable for a further renewal payment until after the end of the 12-month period, or the consumer will not become liable for any further renewal payment but the contract continues beyond the end of the 12-month period. In subsection (7), the “12-month period” means the period of 12 months beginning with the day before the day on which the consumer will become liable for the renewal payment to which the reminder notice relates.

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.
heading_breadcrumb: Arrangements for consumers to exercise right to end contract

commentary.text: S. 260 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: A trader must make arrangements to enable a consumer to exercise a right to bring a subscription contract to an end— in a way which is straightforward, and without having to take any steps which are not reasonably necessary for bringing the contract to an end. A consumer may, alternatively, exercise a right to bring a subscription contract to an end by notifying the trader in accordance with subsection (6) that the consumer is bringing the contract to an end. A consumer may exercise a right to bring a subscription contract to an end at any time permitted by regulations under section 277(1)(c). In relation to a subscription contract entered into online, arrangements under subsection (1) must— enable a consumer to bring the contract to an end online, and ensure that instructions for doing so are displayed online in a place or places that a consumer seeking to end the contract is likely to find them. Arrangements under this section must comply with any other requirements specified in regulations under section 277(1)(c). A notification under subsection (2) may be given by the consumer making a clear statement setting out their decision to bring the contract to an end.

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.
heading_breadcrumb: Duties of trader on cancellation or end of subscription contract

commentary.text: S. 261 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: This section applies where a consumer— has exercised a right under this Chapter to cancel a subscription contract, or has exercised a right to bring a subscription contract to an end. The trader must— give the consumer a notice acknowledging that fact (referred to in this Chapter as an “end of contract notice”), and if an overpayment has been received by the trader from the consumer, refund that overpayment. An end of contract notice must set out— the date on which the contract was or will be cancelled or on which it came, or will come, to an end, and any other information required by regulations under section 277(1)(b). An end of contract notice must be given— in accordance with subsection (5), in writing on a durable medium, and in accordance with any other requirements specified in regulations under section 277(1)(a). An end of contract notice must be given— before the end of such period as may be specified in regulations under section 277(1)(a), or if no such period is specified— in the case of a consumer exercising a right mentioned in subsection (1) by giving a notification online, before the end of the period of 24 hours from the time that the consumer gives the notification; in a case where the consumer exercises such a right by giving a notification in any other way, before the end of the period of 3 working days beginning with the day after the day that the consumer gives that notification. In subsection (2)(b) “overpayment”, in relation to a subscription contract, means any payment made by the consumer for which the consumer is not liable as a result of cancelling the subscription contract or bringing it to an end.

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.
heading_breadcrumb: Rights of consumers to cancel contract for breach

commentary.text: S. 262 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: A trader’s compliance with the following duties is an implied term in every subscription contract— the duty set out in section 256(1)(a) (key pre-contract information); the duty set out in section 256(1)(b) (full pre-contract information); the duty set out in section 258 (reminder notices); the duty set out in section 259(4) to specify in key pre-contract information a reasonable period for the giving of a reminder notice under section 259(3) (timing for the giving of reminder notices); the duty set out in section 260(1) (arrangements for consumer to end contract); the duties set out in section 261(2) (end or cancellation of subscription contract).

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.
heading_breadcrumb: Rights of consumers to cancel contract for breach
Right to cancel for breach of implied term

commentary.text: S. 263 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: This section applies where a trader is in breach of the term implied into a subscription contract by section 262(a), (c), (d) or (e). The consumer has the right to cancel the contract. The right is exercisable by the consumer notifying the trader in accordance with subsection (4) that the consumer is cancelling the contract. A notification under subsection (3) may be given by the consumer making a clear statement setting out their decision to cancel the contract. A subscription contract is cancelled from the time the notification is given. Where a subscription contract is cancelled under this section— the cancellation ends both the trader’s and the consumer’s obligations to perform the contract in respect of any rights or liabilities that would arise (but for the cancellation) after the time at which the contract was cancelled, the consumer’s liability for payments that have arisen under the contract is extinguished to any extent set out in regulations under section 267(1)(b) (and, accordingly, the consumer may be entitled to a refund), and any other provision made under those regulations in relation to the treatment of goods, services or digital content supplied under a cancelled subscription contract applies. No penalty or charge may be imposed on a consumer for cancelling a subscription contract under subsection (2). For further provision about the exercise of a right to cancel under this section, see section 267.

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.
heading_breadcrumb: Right to cancel during cooling-off periods

commentary.text: S. 264 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: A consumer has the right to cancel a subscription contract during— the initial cooling-off period, and any renewal cooling-off period. The right conferred by subsection (1)— is exercisable in any circumstances, and may not be subject to any conditions other than those set out in or under this Chapter. The right is exercisable by the consumer notifying the trader in accordance with subsection (4) that the consumer is cancelling the contract. A notification under subsection (3) may be given by the consumer making a clear statement setting out their decision to cancel the contract. A subscription contract is cancelled from the time that such a notification is given. Where a subscription contract is cancelled under this section— the cancellation ends both the consumer’s and the trader’s obligations to perform the contract in respect of any rights or liabilities that would arise (but for the cancellation) after the time at which the contract was cancelled, the consumer’s liability for payments that have arisen under the contract is extinguished to any extent set out in regulations under section 267(1)(b) (and, accordingly, the consumer may be entitled to a refund), and any other provision made under those regulations in relation to the treatment of goods, services or digital content supplied under a cancelled subscription contract applies. No penalty or charge may be imposed on a consumer for cancelling a subscription contract under subsection (1). For further provision about the exercise of a right to cancel under this section, see section 267.

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.
heading_breadcrumb: Meaning of “initial cooling-off period” and “renewal cooling-off period”

commentary.text: S. 265 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: In this Chapter, the “initial cooling-off period”, in relation to a subscription contract, means the period— beginning with the day the contract is entered into, and ending— in the case of a contract under which goods are supplied, at the end of the period of 14 days beginning with the day after the day on which the consumer receives the first supply of goods under the contract; in any other case, at the end of the period of 14 days beginning with the day after the day on which the contract is entered into. In this Chapter, a “renewal cooling-off period”, in relation to a subscription contract, means a period— beginning with the day on which a relevant renewal of the contract occurs, and ending at the end of the period of 14 days beginning with the day after that day. A “relevant renewal” of a subscription contract occurs for the purposes of subsection (2)— when the consumer becomes liable under the contract for a first renewal payment following the end of a concessionary period, or at any time when the consumer becomes liable under the contract for a renewal payment and either— the consumer will not become liable for the next renewal payment until after the end of the 12-month period, or the consumer will not become liable for any further renewal payment but the contract continues beyond the end of the 12-month period. In subsection (3)— in paragraph (a), “concessionary period” means a period of time mentioned in section 254(3)(a), and in paragraph (b), the “12-month period” means the period of 12 months beginning with the day before the day on which the consumer became liable for the renewal payment. For the purposes of subsection (1)(b)(i), the first supply of goods under a subscription contract is not to be treated as having taken place until such time as the consumer receives all of the goods that the consumer is due to receive as part of that supply. This section is subject to such extensions of a cooling-off period as may be provided for by regulations under section 267(1)(c).

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.

commentary.text: S. 266 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: In relation to each renewal cooling-off period, a trader must give the consumer a notice (referred to in this Chapter as a “cooling-off notice”). A cooling-off notice must set out— that the subscription contract is continuing, that the consumer has a right to cancel the subscription contract during the cooling-off period to which the notice relates, when that period begins and ends, how the consumer may exercise the right to cancel, if the consumer may lose the right, the circumstances under which that will happen, the consequences of the consumer exercising the right, including— any refund the consumer may be entitled to, any reason that refund might be diminished, and in respect of a contract for the supply of goods, whether the consumer will be responsible for returning those goods to the trader, and any other information required by regulations under section 277(1)(b). A cooling-off notice must be given— on the first day of the renewal cooling-off period to which it relates or as soon as reasonably practicable after that day, separately from the giving of any other information, and in accordance with any other requirements specified in regulations under section 277(1)(a).

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.
heading_breadcrumb: Cancellation of contracts under this Chapter: further provision
Cancellation of subscription contract: further provision

commentary.text: S. 267 in force at Royal Assent for specified purposes, see s. 339(2)(c)

text: The Secretary of State may by regulations make provision— about the exercise of the rights of a consumer to cancel a subscription contract under this Chapter; about the consequences that follow a consumer exercising such rights; extending a cooling-off period in such cases, and to such extent, as the regulations may specify. Regulations under subsection (1)(a) may include provision— requiring a right to cancel to be exercised before the end of a specified period; imposing other conditions or restrictions on the exercise of a right to cancel (for example, provision that a consumer may lose the right to cancel a subscription contract during a cooling-off period if they choose to be supplied with digital content or services under the contract during that period). Regulations under subsection (1)(b) may include provision— setting out the extent to which a consumer’s liability for payments that have arisen under a cancelled subscription contract is extinguished; as a consequence of provision made under paragraph (a), requiring a trader to refund a consumer for payments the consumer has made under the contract; treating the consumer as having paid for goods, services or digital content received under a cancelled subscription contract; about the trader’s right to recover goods or digital content that have been supplied under a cancelled subscription contract; setting out the consequences of a consumer— bringing a subscription contract to an end at a time when the consumer has one or more rights to cancel the contract under this Chapter; cancelling a subscription contract at a time when the consumer has more than one right to cancel the contract under this Chapter. Provision under subsection (3)(a) and (b) may secure the result (for example, in cases where a consumer has been supplied with digital content or services under a contract before it is cancelled during a cooling-off period) that— the consumer remains liable (partly or fully) for payments falling due before the cancellation of the contract, and the consumer is entitled to a reduced or no refund. Provision under subsection (3)(e)(ii) must secure the result that, unless the consumer chooses otherwise, the consumer is to be taken to exercise the right to cancel under this Chapter that results in the most advantageous remedy to the consumer (and the regulations may include provision for determining what remedy is “most advantageous” to a consumer in different descriptions of case). Before making regulations under subsection (1)(c), the Secretary of State must consult such persons as the Secretary of State considers appropriate. The following regulations under this section are subject to the affirmative procedure— the first regulations to be made under this section; any other regulations under this section that include provision within subsection (1)(c). Regulations under this section to which subsection (7) does not apply are subject to the negative procedure.

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.
heading_breadcrumb: Offence of failing to provide information about cooling-off rights
Offence of failing to provide information about initial cooling-off rights

commentary.text: S. 268 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: A trader commits an offence if the trader— enters into an off-premises subscription contract, and fails to— give the consumer the information listed in paragraph 11(a) of Schedule 23 in accordance with section 256(1)(a), or give, or make available, the information set out in paragraph 21 of that Schedule in accordance with section 256(1)(b). Subsections (3) and (4) apply where a trader— commits an offence under subsection (1), or would have committed an offence under that subsection but for a defence under section 269, and the commission of the offence, or of what would have been the offence, is due to the act or omission of another person (“P”). P commits the offence (whether or not P is a trader). P may be charged with and convicted of the offence by virtue of subsection (3) whether or not proceedings are taken against the trader. In this section, an “off-premises subscription contract” means a subscription contract— entered into in person, in a place which is not the business premises of the trader, entered into by any means immediately after the consumer was individually and personally addressed by the trader in person in a place which is not the business premises of the trader, or entered into during an excursion organised by the trader with the aim or effect of promoting and selling goods or services to the consumer. In subsection (5), “business premises”, in relation to a trader, means— any immovable retail premises where the activity of the trader is carried out on a permanent basis, or any movable retail premises where the activity of the trader is carried out on a usual basis. In other provisions of this Chapter, references to an offence under subsection (1) include references to an offence under that subsection by virtue of subsection (3).

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.
heading_breadcrumb: Offence of failing to provide information about cooling-off rights

commentary.text: S. 269 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: It is a defence for a person (“the defendant”) charged with an offence under section 268(1) to prove— that the commission of the offence was due to— the act or omission of another person, or reliance on information given by another person, and that the defendant took all reasonable precautions and exercised all due diligence to avoid the commission of such an offence by the defendant or any other person under the defendant’s control. A defendant is not entitled to rely on the defence provided by subsection (1) without the permission of the court unless— the defendant has served on the prosecutor a notice in writing giving such information as was then in the defendant’s possession identifying, or assisting in the identification of, the other person, and the notice is served on the prosecutor at least seven clear days before the hearing of the proceedings or, in Scotland, at least seven clear days before the trial diet.

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.
heading_breadcrumb: Offence of failing to provide information about cooling-off rights
Offences by officers of a body corporate etc

commentary.text: S. 270 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: If an offence under section 268(1) committed by a body corporate is proved— to have been committed with the consent or connivance of an officer of the body, or to be attributable to any neglect on the officer’s part, the officer as well as the body corporate is guilty of the offence and liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly. In subsection (1) a reference to an officer of a body corporate includes a reference to— a director, manager, secretary or other similar officer; a person purporting to act as a director, manager, secretary or other similar officer. If the affairs of a body corporate are managed by its members, subsection (1) applies in relation to the acts and defaults of a member in connection with the member’s functions of management as if the member were an officer of the body corporate. Where an offence under section 268(1) committed by a Scottish partnership is proved— to have been committed with the consent or connivance of a partner, or to be attributable to any neglect on the part of a partner, the partner as well as the partnership is guilty of the offence and liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly. In subsection (4), a reference to a partner includes a person purporting to act as a partner.

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.
heading_breadcrumb: Offence of failing to provide information about cooling-off rights

commentary.text: S. 271 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: A person who is guilty of an offence under section 268(1) is liable— on summary conviction in England Wales, to a fine; on summary conviction in Scotland or Northern Ireland, to a fine not exceeding level 5 on the standard scale. It is the duty of every local weights and measures authority in Great Britain to enforce section 268(1) in its area. It is the duty of the Department for the Economy in Northern Ireland to enforce section 268(1) in Northern Ireland. No proceedings for an offence under section 268(1) may be instituted in England and Wales except by or on behalf of a local weights and measures authority in Great Britain. Nothing in subsection (2) authorises any local weights and measures authority in Great Britain to bring proceedings in Scotland for an offence.

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.
heading_breadcrumb: Information and notices: timing and burden of proof

commentary.text: S. 272 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: This section applies for the purposes of this Chapter. Where a trader gives any information or notice under this Chapter by email, by a message sent online, or by any other means of electronic communication, the information or notice is to be treated as given by the trader, and as received by the consumer, at the time that the communication is sent to the consumer. Subsection (2) applies even if the consumer does not receive the communication where the reason for that is beyond the control of the trader. Subsection (5) applies for the purposes of determining whether a consumer has— given notice that the consumer is cancelling a subscription contract in exercise of a right conferred by this Chapter within the period of time specified for the consumer to exercise the right; given notice that the consumer is bringing a subscription contract to an end within a period of time, or before a date, specified or described in the contract as the period during which, or date before which, the consumer may exercise the right. The consumer is to be treated as having given notice within the required period, or before the specified date, if the communication by which the notice is given is sent before the end of that period or date (and for this purpose it is immaterial whether or not the trader receives the notice). The burden of proof lies with the trader in any dispute between the trader and a consumer as to whether information or a notice has been given by the trader to the consumer in accordance with this Chapter. The burden of proof lies with the consumer in any dispute between the consumer and a trader as to— whether the consumer has notified the trader that the consumer is bringing to an end, or cancelling, a subscription contract in accordance with this Chapter; when the consumer gave such notice. Any information that a trader gives to a consumer under this Chapter must be given in clear and plain language and if given in writing, be in a legible form; if given orally, be audible and comprehensible.

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.
heading_breadcrumb: Terms of a subscription contract which are of no effect

commentary.text: S. 273 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: Any term of a subscription contract that is in contravention of this Chapter is, to that extent, of no effect (including any term that seeks to exclude or restrict a trader’s liability arising from the terms implied into the contract by section 262). In cases to which this subsection applies, any term of a subscription contract which seeks to impose on a consumer liability for a renewal payment before the day on which the contract renews is, to that extent, of no effect. Subsection (2) applies to cases of a description specified in regulations under section 277(1)(e) (and the regulations may include provision for determining when a contract renews in each description of case).

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.
heading_breadcrumb: Other remedies for breach by trader

commentary.text: S. 274 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: Nothing in this Chapter is to be taken as limiting the taking of any other remedies available to a consumer for breach of any term (whether express, implied by section 262 or otherwise) of a subscription contract. Those other remedies may be sought— in addition to the rights conferred on the consumer by this Chapter (but not so as to recover twice for the same loss), or instead of the exercise of any of those rights by the consumer. Those other remedies include any of the following— claiming damages; seeking specific performance; seeking an order for specific implement; relying on the breach against a claim by the trader under the contract; for breach of a term, exercising a right to treat the contract at an end.

act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.

commentary.text: S. 275 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: Subsection (2) applies if— the law of a country or territory other than the United Kingdom or any part of the United Kingdom is chosen by the parties to be applicable to a subscription contract, but the contract has a close connection with the United Kingdom. This Chapter applies in relation to the contract despite that choice. This Chapter does not apply in relation to contracts entered into before section 254 comes into force. Subsections (5) and (6) apply where— a trader enters into a contract that is an excluded contract, but for it being an excluded contract, the contract would have been a subscription contract, and on a later day (the “relevant day”), the contract ceases to be an excluded contract and, accordingly, becomes a subscription contract. This Chapter applies to the contract with the following modifications— sections 256 and 257 (pre-contract information) do not apply; section 258 (reminder notices) applies as if— in subsection (1), the reference to a trader entering into a subscription contract with a consumer that does not involve a concessionary period were a reference to a trader entering into the contract, the reference in subsection (2)(a) to the day that the contract was entered into were a reference to the relevant day, and subsections (3), (4) and (6) were omitted; section 259 (content and timing etc of reminder notices) applies as if, in subsections (3) and (4), references to the period specified by the trader in pre-contract information were references to the period specified by the trader in information given under subsection (6) of this section; section 262 (terms implied into contracts) applies as if— in paragraph (a), the reference to the duty set out in section 256(1)(a) were a reference to the duty set out in subsection (6) of this section; paragraph (b) was omitted; in paragraph (d), the reference to pre-contract information were a reference to the information given under subsection (6) of this section; section 264 (right to cancel during cooling-off periods) applies as if subsection (1)(a) were omitted. As soon as reasonably practicable after the relevant day, and in any event before the end of 12 months beginning with that day, the trader must give to the consumer key pre-contract information and full pre-contract information in relation to the contract, other than any such information that is excluded by subsection (7). Information is excluded by this subsection if— it relates to the initial cooling-off period under the contract; it relates to a period mentioned in section 254(3)(a) (initial concessionary period) and the relevant day falls after the end of that period. For the purposes of the duty under subsection (6)— it is irrelevant whether any of the information required has already been given to the consumer before the relevant day, section 256(5) applies as it applies for the purposes of the duty under section 256(1)(b), and paragraph 13 of Schedule 23 is to be ignored.

commentary.text: S. 280 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: In this Chapter— “business” includes— a trade, craft or profession, any other undertaking carried on for gain or reward, and the activities of any government department or local or public authority; “consumer” means an individual acting for purposes that are wholly or mainly outside the individual’s business; “durable medium” means paper, email or any other medium that— allows information to be addressed personally to the consumer, enables the consumer to store information in a way accessible for future reference for a period that is long enough for the purposes of the information, and allows the unchanged reproduction of information stored; “goods” includes— immoveable property; rights and obligations; water, gas and electricity if they are put up for sale in a limited volume or set quantity; “trader” means a person (“P”) acting for purposes relating to P’s business, whether acting personally or through another person acting in P’s name or on P’s behalf. In this Chapter— references to a contract for the supply of goods, services or digital content include references to a contract for the supply of any combination of goods, services and digital content; references to payment or to a consumer being charged are references to payment, or a consumer being charged, in money or money’s worth; references to something happening automatically under a subscription contract are references to it happening without any action on the part of the consumer to cause it to happen (ignoring the consumer’s action of entering into the contract or any action taken in connection with, or for the purpose of, entering into it); references to something recurring are references to it happening more than once; references to a supply of goods, services or digital content for a fixed term include references to a supply of goods, services or digital content which is fixed to any extent; references to a consumer entering into a subscription contract include references to a consumer placing an order for the supply of goods, services or digital content under a subscription contract in circumstances where— the trader is (in any way) inviting such orders, and the consumer is not required to take any further action for the contract to be concluded.

text: For the purposes of this Chapter, a consumer savings scheme contract is a contract— under which— a consumer makes payments to a trader, the trader credits those payments to an account that is held by the trader for the consumer (“the consumer’s account”), and the payments credited to the consumer’s account provide a fund for the consumer to redeem as goods, services or digital content in accordance with the terms of the contract, to which one or more of subsections (2), (3) or (4) applies, and which is not an excluded arrangement (see section 284). This subsection applies to a contract if it contains terms which have the effect of restricting the times at, or periods of time during, which the consumer may redeem funds from the consumer’s account. This subsection applies to a contract if it contains terms which have the effect of incentivising the consumer to redeem, or refrain from redeeming, funds in the consumer’s account at a time, or during a period of time, specified in the terms of the contract. This subsection applies to a contract if it is marketed or advertised in such a way as to encourage the consumer to redeem, or refrain from redeeming, funds in the consumer’s account at a time, or during a period of time, specified in material used for the purposes of marketing or advertising the contract.

S. 283 in force at 1.1.2026 by S.I. 2025/272, reg. 3

text: In this Chapter, references to a trader operating a consumer savings scheme are references to a trader entering into a consumer savings scheme contract. For the purposes of section 282(1)(a)(ii), it is sufficient for a trader to hold the consumer’s payments in some way other than crediting those payments to a specific account for that consumer and references in this Chapter to a “consumer’s account” are to be construed accordingly. In this Chapter, “protected payments” are payments, made by a consumer under a consumer savings scheme contract, in respect of which funds in the consumer’s account have not been redeemed. Subject to subsection (5), in this Chapter, funds are treated as redeemed when the trader provides the consumer with goods, services or digital content in accordance with the terms of the consumer savings scheme contract. Where a trader provides a consumer with vouchers or credit-tokens which may be redeemed only in respect of goods, services or digital content provided by that trader, funds are treated as redeemed for the purposes of this Chapter only when those vouchers or credit-tokens are redeemed.

A trader operating a consumer savings scheme in the United Kingdom, who is not established in the United Kingdom, must comply with the requirements of this section. References in this Chapter to a trader’s insolvency are references to— a bankruptcy order having been made in relation to the trader (or, in Scotland, the trader’s estate having been sequestrated), a winding up order having been made in relation to the trader as a result of the trader’s insolvency, an appointment of a liquidator (otherwise than following the making of a winding up order) as a result of the trader’s insolvency, the trader being in administration, the appointment of an administrative receiver (or, in Scotland, a receiver) in relation to the trader, or in any jurisdiction, the trader being subject to an order or procedure that corresponds to any order or procedure mentioned in paragraphs (a) to (e).

text: Where a trader relies on arrangements under this section for the purpose of satisfying section 285, the trader must maintain insurance under one or more appropriate policies with an insurer authorised in respect of such business in the United Kingdom, the Channel Islands or the Isle of Man. In this section “appropriate policy” means a policy— under which the insurer agrees to indemnify consumers in the event of the insolvency of the trader; under which consumers are insured persons in respect of the costs referred to in paragraph (d); which does not contain a condition which provides (in whatever terms) that no liability arises, or that any liability arising ceases— in the event of some specified thing being done or omitted to be done after the happening of the event giving rise to a claim under the policy; in the event of the policy holder not making payments under or in connection with other policies; or unless the policy holder keeps specified records or makes available to, or provides the insurer with, information from those records; and which covers the costs of returning to the consumer any protected payments at the time of the insolvency. The trader must meet the costs of arranging and maintaining an appropriate policy and any related charges or taxes, without recourse to the consumer payments which are to be protected under that policy.

commentary.text: S. 287 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)
S. 287 in force at 1.1.2026 by S.I. 2025/272, reg. 3

text: Where a trader relies on arrangements under this section for the purpose of satisfying section 285, the trader must ensure that all payments made by a consumer under a consumer savings scheme contract are held on trust for the consumer, in the United Kingdom, by one or more persons appointed as trustees for the consumer. Subject to subsection (3), the monies are to be held on trust for the consumer as required by subsection (1) until— the funds in the consumer’s account have been redeemed, or any payments made by the consumer in respect of the consumer savings scheme contract have been returned to the consumer. The trustees may authorise the use of monies held on trust for the consumer as required by subsection (1)— to pay suppliers for goods, services or digital content to be provided to the consumer in accordance with the terms of the consumer savings scheme contract, to return payments to the consumer in exceptional circumstances, or to pay any profits after the consumer has redeemed all of the funds in their account. For the purposes of subsection (3)(a), trustees may only authorise the release of monies on receipt of a declaration by the trader that the trader is solvent. The trustee, or where there is more than one trustee, the majority of persons appointed as trustees for the purpose of subsection (1), must be independent of the trader. For the purpose of subsection (5), a person is independent of the trader in relation to a trust only if— the person has no interest in the assets of the trader or of the trust otherwise than as a trustee of that trust, and the person is neither connected with, nor an associate of— the trader, or any person for the time being acting as an insolvency practitioner in relation to the trader. The cost of administering the trust must be paid for by the trader. The trader must arrange for an independent auditor to be appointed to audit the accounts of the trust every three years. In the event of a trader’s insolvency, monies held on trust for a consumer by the trustees in accordance with this section must be returned to the consumer.

S. 288 in force at 1.1.2026 by S.I. 2025/272, reg. 3

text: A trader must, before the end of 30 working days beginning with the day on which a consumer makes the first payment to the trader under a consumer savings scheme contract, provide to the consumer the following information— the name, address, telephone number and email address of the insurer or trustees responsible for protecting the consumer’s payments; where insurance arrangements are in place, the policy number for the policy under which the consumer’s payments are protected; where trust arrangements are in place, a copy of the trust deed under which the consumer’s payments are held. The trader must notify the consumer of any change to any of the information provided under subsection (1) before the end of 30 working days, beginning with the day on which the change takes effect. Where a consumer makes a written request to the trader for the information mentioned in subsection (1), the trader must, before the end of 30 working days beginning with the day on which the request is received, provide, without charge, the information requested. The information provided under this section must be in clear and plain language and, if in writing, in a legible form. The information provided under this section must— in cases where the contract is to be entered into in the simultaneous physical presence of the trader and the consumer, be given in writing on a durable medium; in cases where the contract is to be entered into online without the simultaneous physical presence of the trader and the consumer— be given in writing by being displayed in any location online where the consumer may take steps to enter into the contract, and be accessible in that location without the need for any action by the consumer; in cases where the contract is to be entered into orally without the simultaneous physical presence of the trader and the consumer, be given to the consumer orally and in a way that is audible and comprehensible. In cases not falling within subsection (5)(a) the trader must also, as soon as reasonably practicable after the contract has been entered into, give the consumer the information in writing on a durable medium. A trader operating a consumer savings scheme in the United Kingdom, who is not established in the United Kingdom, must comply with the requirements of this section. It is an implied term of every consumer savings scheme contract that the trader complies with the requirements of this section. The Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013 (S.I. 3134/2013) apply to consumer savings scheme contracts to the extent that requirements under those regulations are not met by compliance with this section.

commentary.text: S. 291 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: This section has effect for the purposes of this Chapter. “ADR” means any method of securing or facilitating an out-of-court resolution of a consumer contract dispute that is carried out by an independent third party acting in relation to both parties to the dispute. But the term “ADR” does not include anything carried out by a person in their capacity as— a judge, or a member of the staff of a court or tribunal. The following are examples of ADR (if carried out as mentioned in subsection (2) in relation to a consumer contract dispute)— mediation; arbitration; early neutral evaluation; action under an ombudsman scheme. In subsection (2) “resolution” includes— a decision binding both parties; a decision which, if accepted by the consumer, binds the trader; settlement of the dispute between the parties. “ADR provider” means a person who does either or both of the following— carrying out ADR in relation to a consumer contract dispute, or making special ADR arrangements. “Special ADR arrangements” are (subject to subsection (8)) arrangements made by an ADR provider with another person (whether or not that other person is an exempt or accredited ADR provider) for ADR to be carried out by that other person in relation to one or more consumer contract disputes. Arrangements made by a person acting for only one of the parties to a consumer contract dispute are not special ADR arrangements. For the meaning of “exempt ADR provider” and “exempt redress scheme” see section 295. “Accredited ADR provider” means a person who is for the time being accredited under this Chapter (whether or not their accreditation is limited to particular descriptions of ADR or special ADR arrangements). In this section “judge” includes— a member of a tribunal, a justice of the peace or, in Northern Ireland, a lay magistrate, a clerk or other officer entitled to exercise the jurisdiction of a court or tribunal, and a holder of any other public office with functions of a judicial nature.

commentary.text: S. 292 in force at Royal Assent for specified purposes, see s. 339(2)(c)
S. 292 in force at 6.4.2026 in so far as not already in force by S.I. 2026/284, regs. 1(2), 2(1)(2)

text: This section has effect for the purposes of this Chapter. “Consumer contract” means (subject to the following provisions of this section) a contract between a trader and a consumer which is— a contract to which Chapter 2 of Part 1 of CRA 2015 (contracts to supply goods) applies; a contract to which Chapter 3 of that Part (contracts to supply digital content) applies; a contract to which Chapter 4 of that Part (contracts to supply services) applies; a mixed contract, that is to say a contract to which any two or three of those Chapters apply (see section 1(3) and (4) of that Act). The reference in subsection (2)(a) to a contract to which Chapter 2 of Part 1 of CRA 2015 applies includes a reference to— a contract between a gas supplier and a consumer for the supply of gas to any premises; a contract deemed by paragraph 8(1) or (2) of Schedule 2B to the Gas Act 1986, or by section 12(1) or (2) of the Energy Act (Northern Ireland) 2011 (c. 6 (N.I.)), to exist between a gas supplier and a consumer for the supply of gas to any premises; a contract between an electricity supplier and a consumer for the supply of electricity to any premises; a contract deemed to exist by paragraph 3(1) or (2) of Schedule 6 to the Electricity Act 1989 or by paragraph 3(1) or (2) of Schedule 6 to the Electricity (Northern Ireland) Order 1992 (S.I. 1992/231 (N.I.1)); the terms applying as between a water supplier and a consumer in respect of the supply of water to any premises by a water supplier. In subsection (3)— “electricity supplier” means a person who is authorised to supply electricity by a licence or exemption under Part 1 of the Electricity Act 1989 or Part 2 of the Electricity (Northern Ireland) Order 1992; “gas supplier” means a person who is authorised to supply gas by a licence or exemption under Part 1 of the Gas Act 1986 or Part 2 of the Gas (Northern Ireland) Order 1996 (S.I. 1996/275 (N.I.2)); “water supplier” means— a water undertaker or a water supply licensee within the meaning of the Water Industry Act 1991, a person supplying water under a water services licence within the meaning of the Water Services etc. (Scotland) Act 2005 (asp 3), or a water undertaker within the meaning of the Water and Sewerage Services (Northern Ireland) Order 2006 (S.I. 2006/3336 (N.I.21)). The reference in subsection (2)(c) to a contract to which Chapter 4 of CRA 2015 applies includes a contract between a heat supplier and a consumer for the supply of heating, cooling or hot water by means of thermal energy provided from a heat network. In subsection (5)— “heat network” has the meaning given by section 216 of the Energy Act 2023, and “heat supplier” means a person who charges for making a supply of heating, cooling or hot water by means of thermal energy provided from a heat network. In the application of provisions of Part 1 of CRA 2015 for determining whether a contract is a consumer contract for the purposes of this Chapter, the following provisions are to be disregarded— section 32(2) (provisions excluded from the operation of section 32(1)); section 48(5) (power to exclude services from scope of Chapter 4 of Part 1). The Secretary of State may by regulations provide that contracts of a description specified in the regulations are excluded from being consumer contracts for the purposes of this Chapter. The power in subsection (8) includes power to provide that the exclusion only applies in circumstances specified in the regulations. Regulations under subsection (8) are subject to the affirmative procedure. “Consumer contract dispute” means a dispute between the parties to a consumer contract which relates to the contract, including a dispute concerning— anything done by either party before making the contract, the making of the contract, obligations under or relating to the contract, or the performance by either party of their obligations under or relating to the contract. In subsection (11) “dispute” means a legal dispute, that is to say one which may be determined by a court or tribunal in proceedings brought by either of the parties to the contract. The “parties” to a consumer contract, or a consumer contract dispute, are the consumer and the trader. The following terms have the meaning given by section 2 of CRA 2015— “consumer” “goods” “trader”. But in interpreting the term “consumer” section 2(4) to (6) of that Act is to be disregarded.

text: A person must not carry out ADR in relation to a consumer contract dispute unless the person— is an exempt ADR provider whose exemption covers the ADR being carried out, is an accredited ADR provider whose accreditation covers the ADR being carried out, or is acting under special ADR arrangements made by— an exempt ADR provider whose exemption covers the making of those special ADR arrangements, or an accredited ADR provider whose accreditation covers the making of those special ADR arrangements. text: In this Chapter— “exempt ADR provider” means a person who— is listed (or of a description of persons listed) in Part 1 of Schedule 25, or is (when carrying out ADR or making special ADR arrangements) acting under or for the purposes of an exempt redress scheme; “exempt redress scheme” means a scheme or other similar arrangement which is listed (or of a description listed) in Part 2 of Schedule 25. The Secretary of State may by regulations amend Schedule 25 for the purpose of— adding a new entry in Part 1 or 2; varying or removing an entry for the time being included in Part 1 or 2; varying the supplementary provision in Part 3. Regulations under subsection (2) may, in particular— provide for an entry in Part 1 of Schedule 25 to apply to a specified person or to any person of a specified description; provide for an entry in Part 2 of that Schedule to apply to a specified scheme or any scheme of a specified description; limit the scope of the exemption given to a person by virtue of an entry in Part 1 or 2 of that Schedule, whether in relation to carrying out ADR or making special ADR arrangements (or both). For the purposes of subsection (3)— descriptions of ADR may be framed by reference to kinds of ADR or types of dispute (or both), and descriptions of special ADR arrangements may be framed by reference to any features of such arrangements, including in particular the kinds of ADR involved or the types of dispute involved (or both). Subject to any limitation on its scope provided for by Schedule 25— an exemption given to a person by virtue of an entry in Part 1 of that Schedule covers anything done by the person in the exercise of the person’s functions that would otherwise be prohibited, and an exemption given to a person by virtue of an entry in Part 2 of that Schedule covers anything done under or for the purposes of an exempted redress scheme that would otherwise be prohibited. In this section— “prohibited” means prohibited by section 293(1) or (2); “specified” means specified in the regulations. Regulations under subsection (2) are subject to the negative procedure.

commentary.text: S. 296 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

S. 296: conferral of functions (6.4.2026) by The Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (Alternative Dispute Resolution) (Conferral of Functions) Regulations 2026 (S.I. 2026/259), regs. 1(2), 3 (with regs. 5, 6)

text: A person who wishes to be an accredited ADR provider must— apply to the Secretary of State for accreditation to enable the person to carry out ADR or to make special ADR arrangements (or to do both), and pay to the Secretary of State the appropriate application fee (if any) prescribed by regulations under section 300. An application for accreditation to carry out ADR may be limited to one or more particular descriptions of ADR. An application for accreditation to make special ADR arrangements may be limited to one or more particular descriptions of special ADR arrangements. An accredited ADR provider may apply to the Secretary of State for their accreditation to be varied by the addition, variation or removal of— any limitation affecting the descriptions of ADR or special ADR arrangements (as the case may be) covered by the accreditation, or any condition on the accreditation. An application under subsection (4) must be accompanied by the appropriate application fee (if any) prescribed by regulations under section 300. The Secretary of State may determine the procedure to be followed in relation to an application for accreditation or an application for the variation of an accreditation. The matters which may be determined under subsection (6) include (among other things)— the form in which applications are to be made; the particular descriptions of ADR for which limited accreditation may be applied for and granted; the particular descriptions of special ADR arrangements for which limited accreditation may be applied for and granted; the information to be given by applicants. Section 295(4) applies for the purposes of subsection (7) as it applies for the purposes of section 295(3). The Secretary of State must publish anything determined under subsection (6) in a manner likely to come to the attention of potential applicants for accreditation. The powers of the Secretary of State under subsection (6) may be exercised differently for different purposes.

long_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of competition in digital markets; to amend the Competition Act 1998 and the Enterprise Act 2002 and to make other provision about competition law; to make provision relating to the protection of consumer rights and to confer further such rights; and for connected purposes.

commentary.text: S. 297 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

S. 297: conferral of functions (6.4.2026) by The Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (Alternative Dispute Resolution) (Conferral of Functions) Regulations 2026 (S.I. 2026/259), regs. 1(2), 3

text: This section applies where an application for accreditation, or for the variation of an accreditation, has been made to the Secretary of State (and has not been withdrawn). In the case of an application for accreditation, the Secretary of State must, as soon as is reasonably practicable— consider the application, decide whether— to grant the accreditation applied for, to grant a more limited accreditation, or to refuse the application, and give notice in writing to the applicant of the decision and, in the case of a decision mentioned in paragraph (b)(ii) or (iii), the reasons for the decision. Accreditation granted under subsection (2)(b)(ii) may be limited to such descriptions of ADR or such descriptions of special ADR arrangements (or both) as the Secretary of State considers appropriate and specifies in the accreditation. If accreditation is granted, the Secretary of State may also decide to impose conditions on the accreditation. The Secretary of State may only grant accreditation if satisfied that the accreditation criteria will be met by or in relation to the applicant after accreditation is granted. An accreditation is not time limited unless— the Secretary of State determines that it is to have effect for a limited period, and the notice of the decision on the application states that the accreditation is time limited and specifies the period for which it has effect. The notice of a decision to grant accreditation must specify the day on which the accreditation takes effect. In the case of an application for the variation of an accreditation, the Secretary of State must, as soon as is reasonably practicable— consider the application, decide whether— to grant the application, to vary the accreditation, but to a different extent than applied for, or to refuse the application, and give notice in writing to the applicant of the decision and, in the case of a decision mentioned in paragraph (b)(ii) or (iii), the reasons for the decision. If the Secretary of State decides to vary the accreditation under subsection (8)(b)(i) or (ii), the Secretary of State may also decide— to impose new conditions on the accreditation, or to vary or remove any existing condition on the accreditation. The Secretary of State may only vary an accreditation if satisfied that the accreditation criteria will be met by or in relation to the applicant after the accreditation is varied. A variation of an accreditation is not time limited unless the Secretary of State determines that the variation is to have effect only for a limited period and the notice of the decision on the application for variation— states that the variation is time limited (unless made permanent following a subsequent application by the ADR provider), specifies the period for which the variation has effect, and makes provision as to the terms of the accreditation in the event that the variation lapses at the end of that period. The notice of a decision to vary an accreditation must specify the day on which the variation takes effect. Where the Secretary of State decides— to impose conditions under subsection (4), or to impose new conditions, or to remove or vary any existing condition on the accreditation, under subsection (9), the notice of the decision on the relevant application must set out the conditions on the accreditation or the accreditation as varied, and give the Secretary of State’s reasons for the decisions made under subsection (4) or (9) (as the case may be). Where an accreditation covers the making of special ADR arrangements, conditions on the accreditation may be framed so as to secure that the accredited ADR provider is responsible for acts or omissions of other ADR providers who carry out ADR under special ADR arrangements made by the accredited ADR provider.

commentary.text: S. 298 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

S. 298: conferral of functions (6.4.2026) by The Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (Alternative Dispute Resolution) (Conferral of Functions) Regulations 2026 (S.I. 2026/259), regs. 1(2), 3 (with reg. 7)

text: This section confers powers on the Secretary of State in relation to the accreditation of an accredited ADR provider. The Secretary of State may, by notice to the ADR provider, revoke the accreditation on the application of the ADR provider. Subsection (4) applies in relation to the ADR provider where the Secretary of State considers that any one or more of the following conditions are met— the ADR provider is contravening, or has contravened, any of the prohibitions in section 293 and 294; the ADR provider is failing, or has failed, to comply with any of the accreditation criteria; the ADR provider is failing, or has failed, to comply with any conditions on its accreditation; the ADR provider is failing, or has failed, to comply with an enforcement notice under section 302. The Secretary of State may by notice to the ADR provider— vary the accreditation, by doing either or both of the following— limiting, or further limiting, the accreditation to such descriptions of ADR or such descriptions of special ADR arrangements (or both) as the Secretary of State considers appropriate, and imposing new conditions on the accreditation, varying any existing condition or removing any existing condition, suspend the accreditation, or revoke the accreditation. In subsection (4)(a)(i) the reference to limiting (or further limiting) the accreditation to particular descriptions of ADR or of special ADR arrangements includes, in particular, limiting it to ADR relating to consumer contract disputes that have already been referred for ADR or to special ADR arrangements that already exist (as the case may be), whether for a limited period or otherwise. Before giving such a notice the Secretary of State must give the ADR provider a reasonable opportunity to make representations as to— whether one or more of the conditions mentioned in subsection (3) are met in relation to the ADR provider, and if so, what action (if any) it is appropriate for the Secretary of State to take under subsection (4). Any variations made under subsection (4)(a) must be variations the Secretary of State considers necessary to secure compliance with the prohibitions in sections 293 and 294, the accreditation criteria, the existing conditions on the accreditation or the enforcement notice (as the case may be). In subsection (7) “existing conditions” means the existing conditions disregarding any previous variations made under subsection (4)(a) or (9)(b). Where variations of the accreditation are made under subsection (4)(a), the Secretary of State must— keep those variations under review, and by notice to the ADR provider vary the accreditation for the purpose of revoking or reversing the effect of all or any of the variations, to the extent that the Secretary of State considers that they are no longer necessary for the purpose set out in subsection (7). A notice that the accreditation is being varied must specify the day on which the variations take effect. A notice that the accreditation is suspended or revoked must specify the day on which the accreditation ceases to be in force. Where the accreditation is suspended the notice must also set out when or in what circumstances the suspension is to cease to have effect so that the accreditation is again in force. The provision required by subsection (12) may consist of any one or more of the following— provision for the suspension to cease to have effect at the end of a period specified in the notice, provision for it to cease to have effect on the satisfaction of conditions specified in the notice, and provision for it to cease to have effect when a decision to lift it is made by the Secretary of State and notified to the ADR provider.

text: The Secretary of State may give an enforcement notice to an ADR provider if satisfied that the provider is contravening, or has contravened, any one or more of the following— the prohibition in section 293(1) or (2); the prohibition in section 294(1) or (3); a condition on its accreditation; the duty to pay a fee due under section 299(1); a duty imposed by regulations under section 303; a duty imposed by a direction under section 304. Before reaching a final view as to whether or not to give an enforcement notice to an ADR provider, the Secretary of State must give the provider a reasonable opportunity to make representations as to— whether the condition in subsection (1) is met, and if so, whether an enforcement notice should be given to it. An enforcement notice is a notice requiring the ADR provider in question to do, or not to do, such things as are specified in the notice or are of a description so specified, with a view to securing compliance with the prohibition, condition or duty in question. An enforcement notice may— include requirements for the ADR provider to give information to the Secretary of State, or include other supplementary, incidental or consequential provision. The notice must make clear, in particular— what requirements are being imposed by the notice, and when they are to be complied with (whether immediately or otherwise). The Secretary of State may, by notice to the ADR provider to whom an enforcement notice has been given— revoke the enforcement notice, or revoke any requirement contained in the notice and, if necessary, make any consequential changes to the other provisions of the notice. The power under subsection (6) may be exercised on the application of the ADR provider or otherwise. An enforcement notice may, with the permission of the High Court or the Court of Session, be enforced as if it were an order made by that court. The Secretary of State may publish information about enforcement notices given under this section.

text: The Secretary of State may by regulations require persons of a specified description (being persons within subsection (2))— to provide ADR information to the Secretary of State; to provide ADR information to a person with functions conferred by regulations under section 307; to provide ADR information to consumers by publishing it.
